_readme: Linux Guardian -- linux/actions.json                                (Phase 6)
THE ACTION REGISTRY. This file is the complete list of things the natural-
language console is allowed to do. If it is not in here, it cannot happen.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL:
Phase 5 already proved the pattern -- app.py has ALLOWED_MODULES, a Python
dictionary, and an HTTP request supplies only a NAME that is looked up in
it. Phase 6 needs the same guarantee, but for actions that take ARGUMENTS,
so the lookup table grows a schema: what each action runs, and exactly what
shape each of its parameters is allowed to be.
The language model NEVER writes a command. It reads this list and returns
one id from it. Everything after that point is ordinary, boring, checked
code -- the same code that runs when the user clicks a button.
WHY THE KEYS BEGINNING WITH AN UNDERSCORE:
JSON has no comment syntax -- there is no '#' and no '//'. The teaching
requirement still applies, so documentation lives in keys the loader
deliberately ignores: any key starting with '_' is skipped by
guardian_actions.py. That keeps the file valid JSON (jq can read it) while
still explaining itself.
FIELD REFERENCE
id            The only name the outside world may use. Matched exactly.
description   Shown in the console's 'available actions' panel.
category      Grouping for the UI only. Never affects permission.
danger        'read'  -> runs immediately, changes nothing.
'write' -> returns a PREVIEW first; only a second, explicit
confirm POST executes it.
script        Filename inside linux/. Resolved by the loader against the
linux/ directory -- the value is never joined with anything
that came from a request. null means the action is served
natively by Python (see 'native').
native        Name of a Python handler, used only when script is null.
args          Fixed argv entries placed BEFORE any parameters. These are
written here by a human, never derived from user input.
select        Which top-level key of the script's JSON answers this
question. null means 'show the whole object'. This is how a
read action can reuse an existing Phase 1 module without
modifying it: system.sh still reports everything, and the
action simply declares which part it is asking about.
params        Ordered list. THE ORDER IS THE ARGV ORDER -- params with
pass_to_script true are appended to the command in exactly
this sequence, each as its OWN argv entry, never joined into
a string.
PARAM FIELDS
name            Key the console and the matcher use.
type            'enum' | 'name' | 'text' | 'day' | 'time'. Chooses which
normaliser runs before validation.
pattern         Python regular expression. Anchored with ^...$ so it must
match the WHOLE value -- an unanchored pattern would happily
accept 'schedule; rm -rf /' because it contains 'schedule'.
required        Whether the action can run without it.
pass_to_script  true  -> becomes an argv entry for the script.
false -> used by Python only (to pick part of the output).
choices_from    Name of a variable in config/guardian.conf whose
space-separated words are the only accepted values. Used
instead of writing service names here, because rule 3 says
the config file is the single source of truth for them.
max_length      Hard cap applied before the regex, so a megabyte of text
can never be handed to a regular expression engine.

actions.description: Report how full the root filesystem is
actions._comment: Wraps the existing Phase 1 system.sh untouched. system.sh keeps reporting CPU, RAM, disk and load exactly as before; 'select' just says which part of that object answers the question 'how full is my disk'.

actions.description: Report RAM usage in percent and megabytes
Report current CPU usage and load average
Report interface, IP, gateway and gateway reachability
actions._comment: select is null because every field network.sh returns is part of the answer to 'is my network working'.

actions.description: Report whether one monitored service is running

params.name: service
params._comment: pass_to_script is FALSE on purpose. services.sh takes no arguments -- it reports every service in MONITORED_SERVICES. So this parameter never becomes part of a command line at all; Python uses it to pick one entry out of the JSON that comes back. An argument that is never passed to a process cannot be an injection, which is the cheapest possible way to be safe. The pattern still runs, because the value is also echoed back to the user.

actions.description: List the top processes by current CPU usage
Run the full health check and return the score out of 100
Show the most recent entries from the Guardian audit log
actions._comment: script is null and this one is served by Python directly. Phase 5's /logs route already reads logs/guardian.log with Path.read_text() and explains why: there is no user input involved, so there is nothing to sanitise, and Python can read a file without starting a process. Inventing a shell script whose entire job is `tail` would add a subprocess and a JSON-escaping problem for no benefit.

actions.description: List the files in the Guardian workspace
actions._comment: The in-sandbox answer to 'is there a file called X'. It reports ONLY on $WORKSPACE_DIR, because that is the only directory this project may touch -- asking about ~/Desktop is not a gap to fill, it is the containment working. danger is 'read': listing a directory changes nothing, so it runs immediately with no confirmation. The fixed arg 'list' is written here by a human and never derived from a request.

actions.description: Start a stopped service that is on the healable list

params.name: service
params._comment: This IS passed to a script, so all three checks apply: the character pattern, the allow-list read from guardian.conf, and then healing.sh itself re-checking PROTECTED_SERVICES and HEALABLE_SERVICES from scratch. Phase 3 does not trust Phase 6, and Phase 6 does not trust the matcher. Deleting any one of these three still leaves the system safe.

actions.description: Create a text file inside the Guardian workspace

params.name: name
params._comment: No dot and no slash are in this character class, which is what stops '../etc/passwd' and 'notes.txt/../../x'. The extension is added by the script, not by the user, so the user cannot choose to write a .service or a .sh file. THE FIRST CHARACTER IS A SEPARATE CLASS ON PURPOSE: it excludes the hyphen, so a name can never be '-rf' or '-f'. A value beginning with a hyphen is not a path to most Unix commands, it is a FLAG, and a validator that allows one is handing an attacker an option rather than a filename. The hyphen is still legal anywhere after the first character, so 'my-notes' works.

params.name: content
params._comment: Free text is allowed -- it is the CONTENT of a file, not part of a command, and it is passed as its own argv entry so a semicolon in it is just a semicolon. The one character banned is NUL, because a C string ends at NUL and a value containing one can mean different things to Python and to the kernel.

actions.description: Create a file on a repeating weekly schedule using a systemd user timer

params.name: name
params._comment: This name becomes part of a unit filename (guardian-<name>.timer), so the same restriction protects ~/.config/systemd/user as well as the workspace.

params.name: day
params._comment: The pattern matches the normalised form, not what the user typed. 'thursday', 'THU' and 'Thu' all normalise to 'Thu' first, which is exactly the spelling systemd's OnCalendar= expects.

params.name: time
params._comment: 24-hour HH:MM. The hour alternation ([01][0-9]|2[0-3]) is what makes 25:00 impossible; a lazier [0-9]{2} would accept it. '12 pm', '12pm' and '12:00' all normalise to '12:00' before this runs.

actions.description: List the schedules this project has created
actions._comment: danger is 'read' -- listing timers changes nothing. The fixed arg 'list' is written here by a human and is not derived from the request.

actions.description: Stop and remove a schedule this project created

params.name: name
params._comment: Only units whose filename starts with TIMER_PREFIX can be cancelled, so this can never disable a systemd unit that a human wrote.
